note.question: How does the benefit experienced by redundant customers adversely affect others who can only join a single line?
note.overview: This paper studies service systems where some (so-called “redundant”) customers join multiple queues simultaneously, enabling them to receive service in any one of the queues, while other customers join a single queue. The improvement in overall system performance due to redundant customers has been established in prior work. The paper addresses the question of fairness—whether the benefit experienced by redundant customers adversely affects others who can only join a single line.

source.quote: Problem definition: We study service systems where some (so-called “redundant”) customers join multiple queues simultaneously, enabling them to receive service in any one of the queues, while other customers join a single queue.
This question is particularly relevant to organ transplantation, as critics have contended that multiple listing provides unfair access to organs for patients based on wealth.
We consider a system with two identical servers, de- noted j ∈{A,B}, each with its own queue.
We illustrate how these findings apply in the organ-transplantation setting through a numerical study using publicly available data.
